claims.text: Rapid solidification induces local Mg segregation in non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys.
The segregated Mg forms metastable Mg-rich intermetallic compounds at grain boundaries and phase interfaces.
Thermal exposure transforms metastable Mg-rich regions into more stable Mg-oxide phases.
The Mg-rich-phase transformation modifies the protective surface oxide layer.
Modification of the surface oxide layer changes corrosion resistance.
Modification of the surface oxide layer changes high-temperature oxidation kinetics.
The initial alloy contains both solid-solution regions and metastable Mg-rich intermetallic compounds.
Controlled thermal aging enhances Mg segregation.
Controlled thermal aging promotes transformation of metastable Mg-rich intermetallic phases into stable Mg-oxide phases.
Thermal aging facilitates localized diffusion of Mg.
Localized Mg diffusion enhances Mg segregation at microstructural interfaces.
Enhanced interfacial Mg segregation drives conversion of metastable intermetallic phases into stable Mg-oxide phases.
The resulting Mg-containing oxide scale is more protective than the oxide scale on the as-cast alloy.
Thermally aged samples will contain more stable Mg-oxide phases at the surface than the as-cast baseline.
Thermal aging will produce a more compact and protective surface oxide layer than occurs in the as-cast state.
Thermally aged samples will exhibit improved corrosion resistance relative to as-cast controls.
Thermally aged samples will exhibit reduced oxidation rates or improved oxide-scale adherence relative to as-cast controls.
The proposed mechanism applies only when aging drives Mg diffusion without causing deleterious coarsening or other harmful transformations.

contradictions.description: The conditions state that the initial non-equilibrium state is maintained during exposure, whereas the structural mediator requires that this initial state evolve through transformation of metastable intermetallic compounds into stable oxide phases.
